h1: Choosing hops for hop water and getting aroma without alcohol
title: Choosing Hops for Hop Water | Craft Beer School
desc: Which hops to use in hop water, how much, hot or cold steeping, pH and carbonation, plus how to keep aroma stable in a drink with no alcohol.
teaser: Hop water is the easiest non-alcoholic drink a brewery can make. Getting it to smell great in week six is the hard part.
standfirst: Hop water is sparkling water flavoured with hops: no malt, no alcohol, almost no calories from sugar. Breweries like it because it uses kit and skills they already have. The challenge is that there is nothing in the glass except water, gas and hop aroma, so every choice about the hop shows.
sections: What hop water is and is not

Hop water is not non-alcoholic beer. There is no malt, no wort and usually no fermentation. It is treated water, a small amount of hops, often a little acid and plenty of carbonation. It should taste dry and refreshing, with a clear hop aroma and very little bitterness.

Because there is no malt sweetness or body to balance anything, flaws stand out. Vegetal or grassy notes, harsh bitterness or stale aroma are all much more obvious than in a pale ale. Our guide to soft drinks and alcohol-free drinks in a brewery covers how hop water fits into a wider range.

Aroma is the whole product, so choose hops that smell great on their own. Popular choices:

  • Citra and Mosaic: tropical fruit and citrus. The most common hop water hops.
  • Amarillo and Cascade: orange and grapefruit, a slightly softer, more familiar profile.
  • Galaxy and Nelson Sauvin: passion fruit and white grape. Distinctive and premium.
  • Saaz or Hallertau types: herbal, floral and gentle. Good for a more refined, less fruity product.

Blends often work better than single hops, because they build a rounder aroma and protect you when one variety is short. Our guide to hop oil chemistry explains which oils give which notes.

Freshness matters even more than in beer. Buy from recent harvests, check the packing date and store pellets frozen and sealed.
Hot steep, cold steep or both

Hot steep. Heat the water to about 80 to 85 °C, add hops, steep for 15 to 30 minutes, then cool. This pulls aroma quickly and helps sanitise the hops. Little isomerisation happens below boiling, but some bitterness still comes through, so watch the contact time.

Cold steep. Add hops to cold water in a tank, much like a dry hop, for 24 to 48 hours. This gives a fresher, brighter aroma with fewer harsh notes, but needs more care with hygiene.

Many producers combine both: a small hot steep for depth, then a cold addition for top notes. Our guide to how hops change aroma covers how temperature shifts the oil profile.

As a starting point, many recipes use roughly 0.5 to 2 g of pellets per litre. Lupulin powders and hop oil products allow lower doses with less vegetal matter, which suits a drink with nothing to hide behind.

Start with clean, low mineral water, usually RO. A small amount of calcium or magnesium can give a slightly rounder mouthfeel, but high mineral content tastes salty in an otherwise empty drink.

Most hop waters are acidified to about pH 3.5 to 4.0 with citric or lactic acid. Lower pH brightens the flavour, softens the perception of bitterness and helps limit microbial growth. Taste trials at a few pH points are worth doing before you lock a recipe.

Carbonation is usually higher than in beer, often around 3 to 3.5 volumes of CO2. The extra sparkle carries aroma to the nose and replaces some of the body a malt drink would have.

Hop water has no alcohol and very little sugar, but it is not sterile. Moulds and spoilage yeasts can grow given time, especially with any sugar or juice added. Low pH helps. Most producers also pasteurise or sterile filter before packaging.

Aroma fades too. Oxygen picked up during transfer and filling stales hop aroma quickly. Warm storage speeds it up. In Indian distribution, where cans may sit in a warm godown or a delivery van, that loss can be dramatic in a few weeks. Purge tanks and cans with CO2, keep dissolved oxygen as low as you can measure and push for cold storage at retail.

Labelling and licensing for non-alcoholic beverages follow food safety rules rather than excise in most cases, but brewery licences and state rules vary. Check with your licensing adviser before you produce on a brewery site.

Start with small trials in kegs. Vary one thing at a time: hop variety, dose, steep method or pH. Run a small tasting panel and keep notes. Then do a shelf-life test: hold samples at room temperature and in the cold. Taste them at two, four and eight weeks. That test tells you more about your process than any recipe.

Hop water looks simple, but making it consistent batch after batch needs a recipe built around aroma, pH, carbonation and stability together. That combination is what turns a taproom experiment into a product you can sell for months.
faqs: What are the best hops for hop water?
Citra and Mosaic are the most common. Amarillo, Galaxy, Nelson Sauvin and noble types also work well, often in blends.
How much hops do you use in hop water?
Many recipes use roughly 0.5 to 2 g of pellets per litre. Lupulin powders and hop oils allow lower doses.
Does hop water need to be acidified?
Most producers acidify to about pH 3.5 to 4.0 with citric or lactic acid. It brightens flavour and helps limit microbial growth.
Why does hop water lose its aroma?
Oxygen pick-up during filling and warm storage stale hop aroma quickly. Keep oxygen low and the product cold.
